en: Abhidhānottaratantra, chapter 27 [Tibetan 30] = Lokesh Chandra facsimile edition = 1138 AD palm-leaf manuscript.
[178.3] [1084] Now I shall fully explain the sādhanā of Ālīḍhāka,
the most excellent of the excellent, who is accomplished from the gnosis of the syllable A.
Eight-faced, sixteen-armed, and three-eyed, he is terrifying and formidable;
his face is made fearsome by protruding fangs, and he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture.
His matted hair is bound with a crescent moon, and he is adorned with a garland of skulls.
He has a crown with a universal vajra at its center; his forehead is adorned with a garland of vajras; he is clothed in a tiger skin;
and his body is embellished with the six mudrās.

Having placed the Bhairava of conceptual construction at the soles of his feet, he treads upon them; he is the subduer of all those who are difficult to tame. He wears a garland of severed heads of obstructors, adorned with various colors.
White and pale in the center, with a slender waist and divine splendor, he was fashioned by Suñja;
likewise, the two right faces are blue and yellow,
while the auspicious left faces are green and reddish-white.
Having seen him— exceedingly white with ashes smeared upwards,
peaceful, filled with the essence of compassion, and graced by the playful movements of his body—
she, who dwells within the bodies of the Ḍākinīs, possesses two arms and a naked form.
Wearing a garland of skulls, with disheveled hair and agitated,
she has three eyes, is deformed and terrible, and is endowed with a girdle of that same color.
Having thoroughly embraced the two [aspects], she is well-established in non-dual yoga.
Having entered into union with the Vajra-bell, she is pressed against the breasts of the goddess;
just as the Ḍāka bestows his mudrā, so too should the Ḍākinī bestow hers.
And with her two arms, she should spread out the canopy of Viṣṇu’s skin.
Holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff,
and bearing a sword and a mallet; possessing three eyes, and likewise a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), an axe, a goad, a noose, the head of Brahmā, a cleaver, and a discus.
In the heart is the most beautiful king of wheels, the twelve-spoked one; there, in the center of its hub, one should visualize Jñānaḍāka,
with his faces, colors, postures, arms, and mudrās exactly as they are.
On the eastern spoke is the ḍākinī named Samayottamā, born from the syllable *i*;
on the syllable *ī* is the ḍākinī named Viśvottamā, who rests upon the northern edge;
on the western side is the ḍākinī named Gaganottamā, joined with the syllable *e*.
In the south is the supreme seat named Pīṭhottamā, where the Ḍākinī resides in the syllable *ai*.
One should place four Ḍākinīs in the four corners starting from the southeast:
the first is the Ḍākinī named Bhīmottamā, located in the syllable *u*.
In the southwest is the ḍākinī named Ghorottamā, joined with the syllable Ū;
in the northwest direction is Vīraḍākinī, joined with the syllable O;
and in the northeast is the ḍākinī named Krodhyottamā, joined with the syllable AU.
In that very square, one should place them starting from the northeast (īśāna) and so forth:
at the letter *ṛ* is the ḍākinī named Siddhottamā;
at the letter *ṝ* is the ḍākinī named Śmaśānottamā.
In the syllable *ḷ* is the ḍākinī named Yogottamā;
in the syllable *ḹ* is the ḍākinī named Caṇḍottamā.
These [deities],
all with white bodies and faces, have two blue and green faces.
The wise one should meditate upon the faces on the left and the right.
Clad in the directions (naked), with disheveled hair, she is terrifying and intent on dancing;
she holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and bears a hand-drum and a curved knife as her supreme weapons.
All of them hold tridents and severed heads, are pale yellow in color, carry goads in their arms,
are mounted upon corpses with shaven backs, and are filled with the essence of compassion.
All of them bear the five mudrās and are adorned with garlands of skull-cups;
all of them wear necklaces of severed heads and produce the sound of the syllable *ala*.
In the syllable AṂ, the Mind-Vajra resides; in the syllable Ā, it becomes the Path of Speech;
in the syllable A, it is the Body-Vajra, situated in the center of the vajra-lotus.
This supreme secret, the most excellent yoga of the ḍākinīs,
was spoken by Vajrasattva when requested by Vajragarbha.
One should summon all the ḍākinīs and place them within the maṇḍala;
then, having beheld the wheel of gnosis through the meditation on the single flavor of the Dharma.
Through the practice of the recitation of knowledge and by means of the excellent mechanism of breath control,
one who is joined with the yoga of the inner self shall cause the supreme multitude of cakras to expand.
Having seen the supreme twelvefold foundation, which is most excellent,
there are twelve stages upon the earth, and thirteen including the vajra-ground.

Pramuditā, Vimalā, Prabhākarī, Arciṣmatī, Sudurjayā, Abhimukhī, Duraṅgamā, Acalā, Sādhumatī, Dharmameghā, Nirupamā, and Jñānavatī—through the purification of these twelve stages (*bhūmi*), the Wheel Goddesses, known as "Supreme Bliss of Great Passion," are present within the stage of Vajrasattva in the midst of the entire assembly. The names of the mantras are preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and the syllable *Hūṃ*;
thereafter, the mantra leader should be joined with the ending syllable *Phaṭ*.

Having visualized the sequence of the wheel of gnosis, consisting of the placement of one's own seed-syllable within one's own heart and joined with body, speech, and mind, they become filled with the single flavor of all things.
Having become silent and composed within and without,
the wise one, well-restrained by breath-control (prāṇāyāma), should cause the recitation being performed to radiate forth.
Oṃ śrī-āliḍāka aḥ āḥ aṃ hūṃ ḍākinījālasaṃvara hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
The yogic self, whose nature is the equality of existence and all phenomena, and who abides in the mantra of the true nature of reality (dharmatā), should enter the dharmadhātu.
Through union with one's own presiding deity, one should worship the yoga of the Self;
and for those whose minds are not concentrated, one should cultivate that [state], for it comes to be.
The emptiness that is the single flavor of the dharmas of mantras, forms, and phenomena;
the selflessness of phenomena, in that all phenomena have the characteristic of being without intrinsic nature.
In the *Abhidhānottara*, the twenty-seventh chapter, the chapter on the sādhana of Ālīḍhāka, the great secret.
[182.2] [Within lacuna 110–112]
